concepts.name: Lunchbox Radio
concepts.tagline: A classic little tabletop radio with a round wooden carry bar between two rounded ears.
concepts.story: Reads instantly as 'the radio'. A big sunflower grille with warm felt behind it, the screen and the five buttons side by side.
concepts.handle: 22 mm beech dowel between rounded side ears. 188 mm grip, 35 mm finger space above the lid. Glued, then pinned by one screw through each ear.
pros: Simplest build: four rectangles, two ears with one curve each, one dowel
Long grip fits a child's two hands or an adult's whole hand
Low, steady box; the screen sits at a comfortable height
cons: Most ordinary look of the three
Needs a 22 mm Forstner or spade bit for the dowel holes

concepts.name: Little House Radio
concepts.tagline: A storybook house: the screen is a window, the buttons are the front door, the speaker sings from the round attic window.
concepts.story: Invites stories and play. Natural birch walls with a painted roof, a rounded chimney that is also the carry handle.
concepts.handle: 22 mm dowel running front to back through two rounded chimney tabs. 88 mm grip, 37 mm finger space above the ridge.
pros: Straight cuts everywhere except the two rounded chimney tabs
Smallest footprint on a shelf (150 x 100 mm)
cons: Tallest (278 mm) on the narrowest base: tips over more easily if pushed
Roof needs a lapped ridge, glue cleats and bevelled wall tops
Opening the back also means unscrewing the dowel end

concepts.name: Cloud Caddy
concepts.tagline: A low, wide radio with a soft cloud-shaped handle on top and a sunny speaker grille.
concepts.story: Calm and sleepy: a cloud to hold and a sun that sings. The battery lies flat on the floor, so it sits very low.
concepts.handle: Cloud fin of three glued 6 mm layers (18 mm thick) with a 100 x 34 mm hand hole, screwed from inside through the lid.
pros: Lowest centre of gravity: hardest to tip over
Carries level: the handle is right above the middle
No bar ends sticking out; one rounded hand hole, nothing to pinch
cons: Three identical curvy layers: most parts (9) and the most coping-saw work
Hand-hole edges need careful rounding on all three layers

common: 6 mm birch plywood; every flat part fits on one A4 sheet, so each prints as one 1:1 template.
Hand tools only: saw with mitre box, coping or fret saw, drill with 3, 3.5, 4, 5, 16 and 22 mm bits (C: a 34 mm Forstner bit or hole saw), sandpaper, clamps, wood glue.
Glued butt joints, no routing. The back is removable with four M3 screws into glued corner blocks, so a tool is needed to reach the battery.
Same electronics as the wooden case: Pi 3 on the back on 8 mm standoffs, 2-inch LCD, five-button board, 40 mm speaker, MAX98357A, ADS, divider, Baseus 5000 mAh, inline USB switch.

Child safety: round every edge (R3 or more), use a toy-safe water-based finish, glue the keycaps onto their stems, keep grille holes 5 mm or smaller with felt behind, keep handle openings 34 mm or more so fingers cannot jam.
Charging works as in the wooden case: open the back and unplug the output lead. A panel-mount USB-C socket is an option for the full design.
